newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban dismiss Afghan alliance, foes' gains.
newsitem.headline: Taleban dismiss Afghan alliance, foes' gains.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban government on Tuesday dismissed an alliance of its adversaries and said its withdrawal from key towns north of the capital did not amount to a defeat of its forces.

Acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference that the Taleban still regarded the two main parties in Monday's alliance, northern leader Abdul Rashid Dostum and former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, as separate.
He said despite the alliance, in which Dostum recognised deposed president Burhanuddin Rabbani and set up a joint council with Masood and others, the Taleban was ready to hold talks with Dostum.

"In the face of any alliance we keep our previous position. In the case of the (Masood) militia that ran away from Kabul, if they submit or hand over the government's property we have no problem with them, and as for the northern forces we are ready to talk to them," he said.

The Taleban, which overran Kabul in a lightning offensive last month before storming north to attack Masood's valley stronghold in the Hindu Kush mountains, have seen much of their gains north of the capital lost in the past week.
The purist Islamic movement has reluctantly admitted losing the key towns of Jabal os-Siraj and Charikar -- the latter an hour's drive from the capital.
Mutaqi denied reports the Taleban had lost the military airbase of Bagram, just north of the capital, and described the withdrawal from towns on the plain as tactical and temporary.
"Concerning the propaganda that our forces have been defeated, it is totally wrong. We have not been defeated, it was only a withdrawal, which took place only for the sake of the people," he said.

Despite taking over three-quarters of the country with their brand of military tactics and hardline Islam, the Taleban have failed to draw any international recognition and now face a coalition of former rivals on their northern flank.

Monday's pact links northern leader Dostum, who has avoided committing his forces to either side in the country's latest conflict, with Rabbani's military chief Masood and other local leaders aligned against the Taleban.

Mutaqi said the situation was calm on Tuesday. But according to witnesses in towns recently taken by Masood's forces, the Taleban counterattacked and at least briefly retook the town of Qara Bagh, 30 minutes' drive from Kabul.

Charikar was bombed on Monday by an unknown aircraft, presumably flying in support of Taleban forces. Nine people were killed and six wounded, Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork reported from the town.
"Now our mujahideen (holy fighters) are well-organised, well-prepared and if the enemy tries to attack they will receive a toothbreaking response from our mujahideen," Mutaqi said.
"Our forces who control a major portion of the country of course can defend one district or one province as well. Our withdrawal cannot be interpreted as a defeat at all."
Kabul itself was calm on Tuesday. Taleban fighters were seen driving through the city in commandeered cars, a familiar sight, and the occasional tank rumbled by. Otherwise life was normal.
Mutaqi said that the recent alliance between Dostum and Masood would not win over the populace and would not succeed.

"I can tell you that making alliances will not solve the problems of Afghanistan and there is a strong Islamic state established here. The people of Afghanistan rejected the (Masood) militia and they will not accept them again," he said.
